specPoints.text: calculate the currents, voltages and resistances of two resistive components connected in a series circuit

primer.text: String resistors together in a row and their opposition to current simply adds up. This note states the series rule for resistance, shows why the supply voltage divides across the chain, and then summarises the full contrast between series and parallel behaviour so that any simple circuit can be solved step by step.

lessons.title: Resistors in series
lessons.opening: Charge pushing through series resistors must run the whole obstacle course, so the oppositions stack. Add the resistances for the total, share the supply voltage across the chain, and one common current threads every component. This lesson turns that picture into three solvable equations.
keyPoints: Resistors in series add: the total resistance equals the sum of the individual resistances.
For two resistors the rule reads R = R1 + R2.
Each extra series resistor adds more opposition for the charge to push through.
The supply voltage divides so that the individual voltages sum to the total.
In series the current is common to every component, so one equation chain solves the circuit.

low.restatement: Total resistance in series is plain addition: R1 plus R2 (plus any more) is the lot.
low.analogy: Toll booths in a row: the total toll is just the sum of every booth's charge.
low.examPointer: Write the full equation R = R1 + R2 before substituting — the marks sit in the statement of the law.

medium.restatement: One current, shared voltage: find the loop current from the total resistance, then read any component's voltage with V = I × R.
medium.analogy: One highway with several tolls: the same traffic (current) passes each booth, and each collects its own share of the total fare (voltage).
medium.examPointer: Check your answer closes: the component voltages you compute must sum back to the supply voltage.

check.stem: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are in series. The total resistance is:

options.explanation: That multiplies the resistances; series adds them.
That subtracts the smaller from the larger.
That is the parallel-pair value, not the series one.

check.stem: Adding a third resistor to an existing series chain:

options.explanation: Series resistances only ever add up.
The new resistor contributes its own share of opposition.
More series resistors means more total opposition.
Direction comes from the supply and never depends on the resistor count.

check.stem: Three resistors of 30 Ω, R and 10 Ω in series give 60 Ω total. R equals:

options.explanation: That adds the total to the known resistors instead of subtracting them.
That only subtracts the 30 Ω and forgets the 10 Ω.
That combines the values in the wrong direction entirely.

check.stem: The voltages across resistors in a series chain:

options.text: add up to the supply voltage
options.explanation: The individual shares always total the supply.

options.text: are each equal to the supply voltage
options.explanation: That is the parallel branch behaviour.
Equal splitting needs identical resistances.

options.text: multiply together to give the supply voltage
options.explanation: Voltage shares add; they never multiply.

check.stem: A series circuit carries a current of 2 A. The current through each of its three resistors is:

options.explanation: The current is not rationed out among series components.

options.text: 2 A shared in some other proportion
options.explanation: Nothing is shared — the same current passes everywhere.
Multiplying the loop current by the component count is meaningless.
One loop means one current: every component carries the full 2 A.

check.stem: Write the equation for the total resistance of two resistors in series.
check.modelAnswer: R = R1 + R2 — the two individual resistances add up to the total.

check.stem: State how the voltages across series components relate to the supply voltage.
check.modelAnswer: They add up: the individual voltages sum to the total supplied by the source.

check.stem: Explain why adding a resistor in series reduces the circuit's current.
check.modelAnswer: Series resistances add, so the loop's total resistance grows; with the supply voltage fixed, the larger opposition leaves a smaller current flowing.

check.stem: A 12 V supply drives a series pair of 4 Ω and 8 Ω resistors. Calculate the current, then the voltage across the 8 Ω resistor.
check.modelAnswer: Total resistance = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω, so I = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 A. The 8 Ω resistor takes V = 1 × 8 = 8 V.

lessons.title: Summary of series and parallel circuits
sourceHeadings: Summary of series and parallel circuits
lessons.opening: Two arrangements, six rules — learn them as a matched set and every simple circuit question becomes bookkeeping. Series keeps one current and adds resistances; parallel splits the current, repeats the voltage, and lands at a total resistance smaller than any branch.
keyPoints: Series circuit: current identical everywhere, voltage shared, resistances added.
Parallel: current splits between branches, voltage identical across branches.
Parallel total resistance lands below the smallest single branch resistance.
A series loop breaks entirely when any component fails.
Series chains need fewer connections than parallel arrays.
Choosing the arrangement means weighing control, wiring effort and failure behaviour.

low.restatement: Series: one current, shared voltage, added resistance. Parallel: split current, repeated voltage, shrunken resistance.
low.analogy: A single-lane road with tolls versus a multi-lane motorway: one queue versus many, and more lanes move more cars with less total delay.
low.examPointer: Memorise the six rules as a table; most two-mark questions are just one rule quoted back.

medium.restatement: The rules interlock: one current in series is why the voltages must share, and the split current in parallel is why each branch keeps the full voltage.
medium.analogy: Two ways to organise a queue at a fair: one line feeding all rides (series) or one ticket booth per ride (parallel).
medium.examPointer: When a question mixes both arrangements, solve the series part and the parallel part separately, then join them at the junction.

check.stem: Which statement about a parallel circuit is correct?

options.text: the current is the same in every branch
options.explanation: Branch currents split; only the voltage repeats across branches.

options.text: each branch receives the same voltage
options.explanation: Every branch sits across the supply and takes the full voltage.

options.text: the total resistance exceeds every branch's resistance
options.explanation: Parallel total resistance is smaller than any single branch.

options.text: the branches share one single loop
options.explanation: Parallel means multiple loops by definition.

check.stem: Which statement about a series circuit is correct?

options.text: the voltage is the same across every component
options.explanation: Series components share the voltage out.
There is nowhere to split in a single loop.

options.text: their resistances add up to one total
options.explanation: Series oppositions simply add up.

options.text: removing one component leaves the rest working
options.explanation: One break opens the whole series loop.

check.stem: A 4 Ω and a 6 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. Their combined resistance is:

options.explanation: Parallel never exceeds the largest branch.
10 Ω is the series answer; parallel lands lower.
Parallel total resistance is smaller than the smallest branch.
Multiplying the resistances has no meaning here.

check.stem: Compared with a single-component circuit on the same supply voltage, a series loop with extra components carries:

options.explanation: More total resistance means less current, not more.
The added resistances throttle the flow at the fixed supply voltage.
The extra opposition must change the flow.
The loop still conducts; only its size changes.

check.stem: Which pairing matches the circuit laws?

options.explanation: Series shares the voltage; parallel repeats it.
Adding resistances is the series law.

options.text: series — resistances add; parallel — voltage the same across branches
options.explanation: Both halves state their arrangement's law correctly.

options.text: series — current splits; parallel — current the same everywhere
options.explanation: Both halves are swapped.

check.stem: State three rules for a series circuit concerning current, voltage and resistance.
check.modelAnswer: The current is the same at every point, the supply voltage is shared between the components, and every resistance adds into the total.

check.stem: State three rules for a parallel circuit concerning current, voltage and resistance.
check.modelAnswer: The supply current splits between the branches, each branch receives the same voltage, and the total resistance is smaller than any single branch's.

check.stem: Explain why the total resistance of two resistors in series exceeds either resistor alone.
check.modelAnswer: The charge must push through both oppositions one after the other, so the two resistances add to a total larger than either individual value.

check.stem: A 6 V cell drives a series pair of 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors. Calculate the total resistance, the current, and the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor.
check.modelAnswer: Total resistance = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω; I = 6 ÷ 6 = 1 A; the 4 Ω resistor takes 1 × 4 = 4 V.

glossary.definition: The single resistance that could replace a whole arrangement — the sum of the parts in series.
A single-loop circuit whose components share the supply voltage and one common current.
A branch circuit whose components each take the full voltage while the current splits between them.
The unit of resistance — one volt driving one amp through the component.

workedExample.prompt: Three resistors sit in series and the combined resistance is 60 Ω. Two of them are 30 Ω and 10 Ω. Find the third resistance.
steps: Write the series law: R = R1 + R2 + R3.

figures.caption: Three resistors connected in series. The total voltage is the sum of the individual voltages, and the total resistance is the sum of the three individual resistances
